name: Urea
lead: Urea (carbamide, CO(NH2)2) is a colorless, odorless, water-soluble compound that is the main nitrogen-containing end product of protein metabolism in mammals, formed in the liver through the urea cycle and excreted in urine. It is practically non-toxic, and most industrial production goes to fertilizer [1]. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler showed that urea could be made from inorganic starting materials, a milestone in the history of chemistry [1].

In dermatology, topical urea is used as an emollient, humectant and, at higher concentrations, keratolytic agent. A 2021 review in Dermatology and Therapy describes its emollient, moisturizing, keratolytic, skin barrier enhancing and antimicrobial properties, and a 2018 review in Dermatologic Therapy covers its use in skin care [2][3]. A US label for a 40 percent urea cream lists indications including dry rough skin, xerosis, ichthyosis, eczema, psoriasis, keratosis pilaris, corns and calluses, and damaged or ingrown nails [4].

Most appearance-related use is in moisturizers and foot or body creams for rough, scaly skin, and in keratosis pilaris. Forum mentions of urea in the sources reviewed mostly concern blood urea as a laboratory marker rather than skin creams.

paras: Urea creams are used for rough, flaky or cracked skin on the feet, hands, elbows and body, and are marketed for bumpy skin such as keratosis pilaris. Low concentrations are described as moisturizing, while higher concentrations soften thick scale and calluses [2][3][4].

A US 40 percent urea cream label lists debridement and promotion of healing of hyperkeratotic lesions, including where healing is slowed by infection, necrotic tissue or debris, and states that urea is useful in conditions such as dermatitis, psoriasis, xerosis, ichthyosis, eczema, keratoderma, corns, calluses and diseased nails [4].

Urea is also studied in other medicine. Registered trials examine oral urea for hyponatremia caused by SIAD or subarachnoid hemorrhage and oral urea as a stimulus in testing polyuria-polydipsia [5][6][7][8]. Topical urea cream has been tested to prevent capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome in cancer patients [9][10].

The 2021 review summarizes multiple lines of evidence for emollient, moisturizing, keratolytic, barrier-enhancing and antimicrobial properties [2]. In a registered phase 3 trial, 12 percent ammonium lactate was compared with 10 percent urea cream in 40 older adults with xerosis [11]. A 2025 randomized trial of a urea-based cream to prevent hand-foot syndrome with capecitabine was published in BMC Cancer [9]; a related phase 2/3 trial of urea cream with the same aim was registered with 214 participants, and a phase 2 trial tested topical diclofenac for the same syndrome [10][12].

The US label for a 40 percent urea cream lists transient stinging, burning, itching or irritation as adverse reactions that normally disappear when use stops, and warns for topical use only and to avoid contact with eyes, lips and mucous membranes [4]. Wikipedia describes urea as practically non-toxic [1].

Topical urea is described as binding water as a humectant and, at higher concentrations, as loosening hydrogen bonding in keratin to help shed dead skin, with reported effects on barrier function and antimicrobial peptide expression [2][3]. Physiologically, urea is produced in the liver from ammonia and carbon dioxide and plays a central role in nitrogen excretion [1].

Urea is the simplest amide of carbamic acid and is dissolved in water as a neutral solution. More than 90 percent of industrial production goes to agriculture as a nitrogen fertilizer [1]. The name comes from the Greek word for urine, and Wöhler's 1828 synthesis challenged the doctrine of vitalism, which held that organic compounds could come only from living organisms [1]. A 2014 review covers urea's biochemistry [13].

On T Nation, urea is discussed mainly as a blood test result. Users post lab panels showing urea or BUN, and others describe urea as a product of protein breakdown after training or high protein intake [14][15][16]. These threads concern physiology and lab interpretation, not skin products.

Topical urea has been studied in dry skin and in oncology supportive care. Studies include the 40-participant ammonium lactate versus urea cream trial in xerosis [11], a 2025 randomized trial of urea cream for capecitabine hand-foot syndrome [9], and a 214-participant registered phase 2/3 trial with the same aim [10]. Reviews summarize the broader dermatology literature [2][3].

Other human work concerns systemic urea: terminated and ongoing trials for hyponatremia [5][6][8], a copeptin study in healthy adults and patients with polyuria-polydipsia [7], and the urea-to-creatinine ratio as a biomarker of catabolism in critical illness [17]. These are unrelated to cosmetic use.
